classifications.label: Systematic calibration or zero-point offset between lab and observational setups
Environmental or instrumental drift is coupled across instruments but manifests differently in lab vs observational settings
Observational instruments are measuring noise or a different physical phenomenon than lab instruments
Cross-instrument calibration has drifted or been inadequately established during baseline period
Observational instruments are experiencing transient environmental or instrumental disturbance on Days 19–20 that lab instruments are shielded from

Lab and observational instruments are measuring the same physical quantity but with different gain or zero-point calibration, and the weak cross-correlations reflect this scale mismatch rather than uncorrelated noise

The 10-day baseline period was insufficient to establish true zero-point or gain calibration; inter-instrument synchronization was not verified from day 1, and apparent drift is an artifact of incomplete baseline establishment
Observational instruments are inherently noisier or lower-fidelity than lab instruments and are not suitable for this precision program; they should be re-engineered or retired

A systematic synchronization or clock error between lab and observational data streams was introduced during acquisition or logging, causing apparent time lags and sign reversals in cross-correlations
Day 30 pendulum_lab excursion is a transient environmental or mechanical disturbance localized to the lab instrument, unrelated to observational setup or settlement-wide physics

The pendulum_lab baseline (n=118 over Days 1–10) was not truly representative; the Day 30 readings reveal an underlying slow drift that was not detectable in the baseline window but is now becoming visible in the tail of the distribution

Pendulum_lab was recalibrated or adjusted on Day 30 morning; the two new readings reflect a real change in instrumental reference (zero-point shift), and all prior baseline and post-baseline readings were made with a different physical setup

Environmental signal (thermal, barometric, or gravitational) is beginning to emerge at a 25–30 day period; pendulum_lab is more sensitive to this signal than resonator_lab due to its lower mechanical stiffness, and the Day 19–20 observational anomalies were an earlier phase of the same phenomenon
Logging, timestamping, or trial-numbering error on Day 30: the two anomalous pendulum_lab readings belong to a different day or a different instrument, or their timestamps are mislabeled

All four instruments are measuring independent physical quantities or instrumental noise rather than a common signal; the measurement programme is not coupled to a shared environmental or physical phenomenon

Baseline period (n=10 days) was too short to capture true instrumental behaviour; each instrument has a distinct drift timescale (15–40 days) that was not yet visible in Days 1–10, and correlations are weak because instruments drift out of phase with each other

At least one instrument (likely observational channel) has a systematic calibration error or zero-point offset undetected in baseline; the observational instruments are not reliably coupled to the lab instruments due to systematic rather than random error

The measurement campaign is correctly executed and instruments are independent; weak correlations are expected because Meridian does not experience a large common environmental signal, or the signal is much smaller than instrumental noise

Data aggregation or correlation method is flawed; the lag-based cross-checks (4–6 day offsets) are artifacts of finite sample size and incorrect alignment; true correlations are masked by poor methodology
